verdicts.finding_id: exp-rep1::5::scripts/accept-release.sh:229 — the fabricated-sha claim sweep is defeated by an adjective. CLAUSE treats bare ` but ` as a clause boundary, but ` but ` also coordinates *inside* a noun phrase, and when it does it splits the claim's two halves into different clauses so neither carries both stems. Demonstrated on a clean clone of exp-rep1: appending `It detects a well-formed but fabricated sha and stops the phase.` to three-loop-workflow/references/build.md printed `ACCEPT: all checks passed`, exit 0, zero FAIL lines. That is the check's own target verb and noun, in the vocabulary the protected passage itself uses (build.md:218 reads "a well-formed sha it never created"), and it is the same defect class as A1/A1b/A1c — a positive claim landing beside the negation — reached through the splitter rather than around it. The reverse adjective order (`a fabricated but well-formed sha`) IS caught, which confirms the splitter is the cause and not the CLAIM regex. No case in scripts/negative-test-accept.sh probes an intra-phrase coordinator; the same exposure exists for ` while ` and ` though `, which are also in CLAUSE and also occur non-clausally.

votes.why: Reproduced end-to-end at 77cda1b: appending `It detects a well-formed but fabricated sha and stops the phase.` to build.md gives `ACCEPT: all checks passed`, exit 0, 0 FAIL, and so do `a valid but fabricated sha` / `a plausible but fabricated sha` — the latter two DO match CLAIM on the unsplit sentence, so the CLAUSE ` but ` split (accept-release.sh:229-230, new in this diff) is an independent sufficient cause; reverse order fails, nothing in the file discloses intra-phrase coordination, and no A/B case in negative-test-accept.sh probes it. (Only nit: for the headline sentence the hyphen in "well-formed" also blocks CLAIM's `[\w'`*]+` token class, so the claim's "confirms the splitter is the cause and not the CLAIM regex" is imprecise for that one sentence — the hyphen-free variants still prove the point.)

Reproduces, but bare " but " is in CLAUSE precisely because pinned case A1c ("The manual path cannot do this, but the script detects a fabricated sha...") requires it — removing it reopens a demonstrated bypass; I confirmed the reverse adjective order and every natural correction (A2/A2b/A2c/A2d wordings) still FAIL, so this is a documented tradeoff of a regex clause splitter on one contrived attributive coordination, not lost coverage.
